subChunks.title: Badges, Tags, and Status Indicators
subChunks.hookHtml: Badges, tags, and status indicators are the micro-components that communicate state, category, and metadata at a glance. They appear in navigation bars, card headers, table rows, and list items. Getting them right means consistent sizing, semantic colour choices, and proper inline alignment — all achievable with Tailwind's compact utility sets.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Badge anatomy

/* The universal badge base */
inline-flex items-center
px-2 py-0.5
rounded-full
text-xs font-medium

Semantic colour variants

/* Success / Active */
bg-emerald-100 text-emerald-700

/* Warning / Pending */
bg-amber-100 text-amber-700

/* Error / Critical */
bg-red-100 text-red-700

/* Info / Default */
bg-blue-100 text-blue-700

/* Neutral / Secondary */
bg-gray-100 text-gray-600

/* Premium / Special */
bg-purple-100 text-purple-700

Badge with icon

<span class="inline-flex items-center gap-1 px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full text-xs font-medium
             bg-emerald-100 text-emerald-700">
  <svg class="w-3 h-3" ...>...</svg>
  Active
</span>

Status dot (colour only)

<span class="flex items-center gap-2">
  <span class="w-2 h-2 rounded-full bg-emerald-500"></span>
  Online
</span>

Notification count badge on avatar

<div class="relative inline-block">
  <img class="w-10 h-10 rounded-full" src="..." alt="" />
  <span class="absolute -top-1 -right-1
               w-5 h-5
               bg-red-500 text-white
               text-xs font-bold
               rounded-full flex items-center justify-center">
    3
  </span>
</div>

Tier/level badge (outlined style)

<span class="inline-flex items-center px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full text-xs font-medium
             border border-amber-300 text-amber-700 bg-transparent">
  Apprentice
</span>

Tag list (dismissible)

<div class="flex flex-wrap gap-2">
  <span class="inline-flex items-center gap-1 px-3 py-1 rounded-full text-sm
               bg-gray-100 text-gray-700 font-medium">
    React
    <button class="ml-1 text-gray-400 hover:text-gray-600" aria-label="Remove React">
      ×
    </button>
  </span>
</div>

Progress bar

<div class="w-full bg-gray-200 rounded-full h-2">
  <div class="bg-blue-600 h-2 rounded-full transition-all duration-300"
       style="width: 60%"></div>
</div>

Sable: "Badges communicate state — they must be coloured semantically, not aesthetically. Green = success/active. Amber = warning/pending. Red = error/critical. If you use red for a 'Featured' badge just because it looks bold, you've broken the semantic contract. Your users will worry about something being wrong."

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Badges are the punctuation of a UI — small, precise, and loaded with meaning. Green means go. Amber means caution. Red means danger. Use them right and users read the page without thinking. Use them wrong and you'll have confused support tickets before Friday.

storyBeats.speaker: The six semantic badge variants
storyBeats.text: Active Pending Critical Info Draft Premium

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a status badge system and a member card with badges:

  • .badge: inline-flex, items-center, px-2, py-0.5, rounded-full, text-xs, font-medium
  • .badge-success: bg-emerald-100, text-emerald-700
  • .badge-warning: bg-amber-100, text-amber-700
  • .badge-error: bg-red-100, text-red-700
  • .badge-info: bg-blue-100, text-blue-700
  • .progress-bar: w-full, bg-gray-200, rounded-full, h-2
  • .progress-fill: bg-blue-600, h-2, rounded-full, transition-all

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a quest status dashboard row from scratch showing: a quest title, a difficulty badge (colour-coded by difficulty), an XP reward badge, a status indicator (dot + text), and a progress bar. Create at least four different status variants. No starter code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the semantic meaning behind badge colours — why are green, amber, red, and blue the standard choices and what does each communicate? Walk through the notification count badge on an avatar — why does it need relative on the parent and absolute on the badge, and how do negative positioning values (-top-1, -right-1) work?

questions.prompt: Which class combination creates the standard badge base that aligns icon and text horizontally with a rounded pill shape?
options: inline-flex items-center px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full text-xs font-medium
flex items-center px-2 py-1 rounded text-sm
questions.answer: inline-flex items-center px-2 py-0.5 rounded-full text-xs font-medium
questions.explanation: inline-flex allows the badge to sit inline with text (unlike block flex). items-center vertically aligns icon and text. rounded-full creates the pill shape. px-2 py-0.5 provides tight but readable padding. text-xs and font-medium are the standard badge type treatment.

questions.prompt: A progress bar needs its fill div to smoothly animate when the percentage changes. Which class on the fill div achieves this?
questions.explanation: transition-all transitions all CSS properties including width. When the width changes (via style prop or class update), the fill animates over 300ms. Tailwind doesn't have a transition-width utility — you must use transition-all (or the arbitrary form transition-[width]) to animate width changes.

questions.prompt: A designer uses a bold red badge for a 'Featured Quest' label (not an error or warning — just emphasis). What is the problem with this choice?
options: Red is semantically associated with errors and danger — users will read the badge as indicating a problem, creating confusion and anxiety rather than emphasis
Red badges don't render correctly on dark backgrounds
The bg-red-100 variant is too light to be used for emphasis
Red is fine for any purpose — colour meaning is purely cultural and varies by user
questions.answer: Red is semantically associated with errors and danger — users will read the badge as indicating a problem, creating confusion and anxiety rather than emphasis
questions.explanation: Colour carries semantic meaning in UI design. Red universally signals danger, error, or required action. Using it for a neutral label like 'Featured' breaks the semantic contract and causes users to mentally process 'what's wrong here?' before understanding the intent. Use purple or amber for emphasis/featured states.
